corrections.source_says: Use other (controlled classroom comparison with allocation to AI unspecified), rather than field_rct. The paper explicitly randomizes students into brainstorming groups and later pairs groups randomly for idea selection, but does not state how ChatGPT access was allocated. Retain assignment.randomized='not_stated' and criterion_1_random_assignment_of_ai='unclear'. The false randomized-study flag means random AI assignment is unconfirmed, not that nonrandom assignment is proven; context_class='none' remains provisional for the same reason.
corrections.quote: For a two-week time period, a cohort of 33 students was randomly assigned to 8 brainstorming groups, comprising 3 to 5 students per group.
corrections.locator: PDF p. 4, Education context & dataset description, first and final paragraphs; p. 5, continuation before Table 2

confirmed: Source: the complete 13-page ASEE 2024 proceedings PDF, Paper ID #43798; title and all eight authors match the form (PDF p. 1 and PDF metadata). The markdown was read in full, and all PDF pages were checked; references end on p. 13, with no appendix or supplement identified.

One original classroom study, not a synthesis or an AI-only versus human-output comparison: students revised ChatGPT suggestions into submitted product ideas (PDF pp. 5-6, Quantitative analysis & discussion). Synthesis fields appropriately remain empty.

The cohort consists of 33 graduate students in a product engineering course in the western United States in spring 2023, randomly placed into eight groups of three to five (PDF p. 4, Education context & dataset description). This is the reported count at group formation, not a separately confirmed count randomized to AI access.

Table 2 lists GA group counts 5, 3, 5, 4 and GB counts 4, 4, 4, 4, with combined-group totals 9, 7, 9, 8. The form transparently derives 17 GA and 16 GB students by column sums; these are people, not ideas or ratings, and no exclusions are stated (PDF p. 5, Table 2; p. 4, cohort description).

The 33-person dataset is below 50, so criterion_2_at_least_50_people=not_met and eligibility.core=no are supported irrespective of the unresolved AI allocation (PDF pp. 4-5, cohort description and Table 2).

Half the groups had ChatGPT through Microsoft Teams under the name iBot, and half had no ChatGPT; no model version is stated. Each group submitted ten product ideas weekly for two weeks, and combined groups selected five most creative ideas from twenty (PDF pp. 4-5, Table 1, Figure 1 and study procedure).

Creativity is scored on submitted output through peer selection, and diversity is computed from submitted ideas, supporting criterion_3_outcome_scored_on_output=met (PDF p. 6, Research question #1; pp. 8-9, Research question #2).

For perceived creativity, the paper prints E[RA]=0.725, an average of 3.625 ChatGPT-assisted ideas among the five selected, and Wilcoxon signed-rank p=0.012 against 0.5. Regression p-values for week, group and GA student share are 0.444, 0.397 and 0.411, respectively (PDF p. 6, Research question #1).

Preprocessed idea length is 14.92 words with ChatGPT versus 10.5 without it, described as statistically significant at the 0.001 level. Unique-word counts are 573 versus 376 over two weeks, and Jensen-Shannon divergence is 0.4094 (PDF p. 7, Research question #1, paragraphs around Figure 3).

The diversity measure pools each group's ten weekly ideas into one TF-IDF vector and compares pairwise cosine distances within each arm; reported t-test p-values are 0.9624 for week 1 and 0.3375 for week 2 (PDF p. 9, Research question #2). These are comparisons of group pairs, not independent individual-student scores.

The form correctly preserves and flags a source inconsistency: the prose claims distances range from 0.8 to 0.92, although Figure 6 includes 0.45, 0.58, 0.63, 0.67 and 0.75 (PDF p. 9, final paragraph; p. 10, Figure 6).

All numbers in the one-line finding match the cited PDF passages: 0.725, five selected ideas, the 0.5 null, p=0.012, and diversity p=0.9624 and 0.3375 for weeks 1 and 2. The diversity tests report no statistically significant difference (PDF pp. 6 and 9).
summary: The paper documents random group formation but does not establish random assignment of ChatGPT access, so the field_rct label should be replaced by other with allocation left not_stated. The 33-student sample and all reported numerical findings match the PDF, including the prose-Figure 6 discrepancy already flagged in the form.
